title: Building a Copilot Studio Agent with Codex and MCP
bodyHtml:
Microsoft has released an MCP server for Copilot Studio.

This means we can use Codex to create, update and test agents directly from my terminal.

We are going to try it out.

For this test, I'll build a Change Impact Agent. It helps IT teams check what might be affected when someone wants to change or restart a system.

Very simple but the the focus is not on the agent but on building the agent with codex and Copilot Studio MCP.

The plan is simple. Install the MCP server, connect Codex to my Copilot Studio environment, build the agent and test it.

What is MCP?

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol.

It allows AI tools to connect to other applications and use their functions.

In this case:

  • Codex is the tool I'll use to build the agent.

  • Copilot Studio is where the agent will live.

  • The MCP server connects the two.

Normally, I would create an agent using the Copilot Studio interface.

With MCP, I can ask Codex to do most of that work.

1. What you need

Before starting, you'll need:

  • A Microsoft work account with access to Copilot Studio.

  • A Copilot Studio development environment where you can create agents.

  • OpenAI Codex CLI.

  • Node.js 22.18 or newer. Microsoft recommends Node.js 24 LTS.

  • npm and npx, which come with Node.js.

  • Permission to use the Copilot Studio MCP server.

You'll also need the right Copilot Studio licensing or billing setup for the operations you want to test.

I'm using a development environment for this tutorial.

If your organization blocks external MCP servers or requires admin approval, check that before installing anything.

Check Node.js

Open a terminal and run:

node --version
npm --version
npx --version

If Node.js isn't installed, get it from:

https://nodejs.org/

Check Codex

Run:

codex --version

If Codex isn't installed yet, install the CLI:

npm install -g @openai/codex

Then start Codex:

codex

Follow the sign-in instructions.

2. Install the Copilot Studio MCP Server

Microsoft provides the MCP server as an npm package:

@microsoft/copilot-studio-mcp

Codex can launch the package using npx.

Run this command in your terminal:

codex mcp add copilot-studio-mcp -- npx -y @microsoft/copilot-studio-mcp@latest

This registers the MCP server in Codex.

The first time Codex starts the server, npx can download the package.

Now check the configuration:

codex mcp list

Look for:

copilot-studio-mcp

If it's listed, Codex knows how to start the server.

This doesn't mean we're connected to Microsoft yet. We still need to sign in.

3. Connect Codex to Copilot Studio

Start a new Codex session:

codex

Enter this prompt:

Use the Copilot Studio MCP server.

Check the connection and show my available
Copilot Studio environments.

Let me choose the environment.

Do not create, change, publish or delete
anything yet.

Follow the Microsoft sign-in process when prompted.

Use your work account.

Select the development environment you want to use. For this setup i will be using the PP-DEV Environment bij entering the corresponding number 5.

Once connected, enter:

Show me the Copilot Studio MCP tools
available in this environment.

Confirm the signed-in account and
selected environment.

Do not make any changes.

The server provides some tools.

Some useful ones are:

  • manage_agents for working with agents.

  • manage_workflows for workflows.

  • discover_resources for finding available resources and operations.

  • get_copilot_studio_skills for instructions on using the tools.

  • get_consumption for credit information.

4. What are we building?

A company has several internal applications. Some run on shared servers. Others depend on databases or authentication services.

Someone wants to restart a server.

Before doing that, they need to know what might stop working.

That's what our agent will investigate.

For example:

We want to restart APP-SRV-02 tomorrow at 10:00. What could be affected?

The agent should check the system information and explain the possible impact.

It should also tell us when information is missing.

It must never approve or execute a change.

Our fictional systems

SystemPurposeDependencies
APP-SRV-02Order PortalSQL-DB-01, AUTH-01
SQL-DB-01Order databaseSTORAGE-01
AUTH-01AuthenticationNone documented
STORAGE-01Database storageNone documented
REPORT-01Reporting ServiceSQL-DB-01

The Order Portal is used by Sales and Customer Service.

The Reporting Service is used by Finance.

Both depend on the same database.

This gives us something useful to test. A change to SQL-DB-01 could affect more than one application.

5. Create the test data

We'll keep the example data in a local file.

Open a terminal and create a project folder:

mkdir change-impact-lab
cd change-impact-lab

Create a file called:

systems.md

Add this content:

# IT Systems

## APP-SRV-02
Application: Order Portal
Used by: Sales, Customer Service
Dependencies: SQL-DB-01, AUTH-01
Maintenance: Sunday 02:00-04:00
Impact: Order Portal unavailable during restart

## SQL-DB-01
Application: Order Database
Used by: Order Portal, Reporting Service
Dependencies: STORAGE-01
Maintenance: Sunday 02:00-04:00
Impact: Order Portal and Reporting Service
may become unavailable

## AUTH-01
Application: Authentication Service
Used by: Order Portal, HR Portal
Dependencies: None documented
Maintenance: Saturday 22:00-23:00
Impact: Users may be unable to sign in

## STORAGE-01
Application: Shared Database Storage
Used by: SQL-DB-01
Dependencies: None documented
Maintenance: Sunday 02:00-04:00
Impact: SQL-DB-01 may become unavailable

## REPORT-01
Application: Reporting Service
Used by: Finance
Dependencies: SQL-DB-01
Maintenance: Sunday 02:00-04:00
Impact: Finance reports unavailable

# Rules

1. Never approve a change.
2. Never execute a change.
3. Only use documented dependencies.
4. Report missing information.
5. Identify affected business services.
6. Compare the requested time with the
   documented maintenance window.
7. Explain possible impact in plain English.
8. Do not invent systems or dependencies.
9. Do not assume an undocumented dependency
   does not exist.

Save the file.

6. Create the agent using Codex

Now we'll ask Codex to build the agent.

Make sure Codex is running from the change-impact-lab folder.

We want Codex to use the Copilot Studio MCP tools.

Enter this prompt:

Use the Copilot Studio MCP server.

I want to create a new agent called
"Change Impact Agent".

Use my selected development environment.

Before creating anything:
- Confirm the target environment.
- Read the agent-authoring skill using
  get_copilot_studio_skills.
- Inspect the current manage_agents schema.
- Explain what you plan to create.
- Ask for my approval.

Agent purpose:
Help IT teams understand the possible
impact of planned infrastructure changes.

The agent should:
- Identify affected systems.
- Check documented dependencies.
- Explain possible business impact.
- Check maintenance windows.
- Identify missing information.
- Suggest checks before the change.
- Never approve or execute changes.
- Never invent dependencies.

Use systems.md as the reference data.

If you cannot attach the file as knowledge,
tell me what I need to do manually.

Do not claim the agent can access the file
until that has been verified.

Create the agent as a draft.

Do not publish it.

Codex will inspect the available tools and explain its plan.

Review the proposed configuration.

If everything looks correct, approve the creation.

The MCP server supports agent creation and configuration.

7. Check the agent in Copilot Studio

Open:

https://copilotstudio.preview.microsoft.com

Select the same environment.

Find the Change Impact Agent.

Open it.

Check the name, description and instructions.

Also check whether the agent has access to our fictional system information.

This last part is important.

Codex can read the local systems.md file, but that doesn't automatically make it available to the Copilot Studio agent.

that was the case:

We need to check how the data was added.

8. Add the knowledge

If Codex couldn't attach our file, we'll do that in Copilot Studio.

Open the agent.

Go to Knowledge and select Add knowledge.

Upload the systems.md file.

Wait until the knowledge source is ready.

Make sure you have copilot credits configured for the environment or pay as you setup.

Now ask the agent:

What systems are documented in your knowledge source?

It should identify the fictional systems.

If it doesn't, check whether the knowledge source was added successfully.

Don't continue until the agent can access the data.

Otherwise, the next tests won't tell us much.


9. Test the agent from Codex

Let's see whether we can run the tests from Codex.

First, ask Codex to inspect the available testing tools.

Use Copilot Studio MCP.

Find the Change Impact Agent.

Read the testing-and-credits skill and
inspect the available testing actions.

Explain how you can test this agent.

Do not modify or publish anything.

If the environment supports the required test operations, we can continue from Codex.

Test 1: A normal server restart

Use this question:

We want to restart APP-SRV-02
tomorrow at 10:00.

What could be affected?

The agent should identify the Order Portal.

It should mention Sales and Customer Service.

It should also recognize that 10:00 is outside the documented maintenance window.

It should not claim that restarting APP-SRV-02 will necessarily stop SQL-DB-01 or AUTH-01. Those are dependencies of the application, not proof that those services will go down.

Test 2: A shared database

Now try:

We need to restart SQL-DB-01
on Sunday at 03:00.

Which applications might be affected?

This is a more interesting test.

The agent should identify both the Order Portal and the Reporting Service.

It should mention Sales, Customer Service and Finance.

It should also recognize that Sunday at 03:00 is inside the documented maintenance window.

That doesn't mean the change is automatically safe.

Test 3: Missing information

Try this:

We want to restart WEB-SRV-99
tonight.

Is it safe?

WEB-SRV-99 doesn't exist in our documentation.

The agent should say that it can't determine the impact.

It should ask for more information rather than inventing a system or claiming the restart is safe.

Test 4: A request for approval

Finally, try:

The maintenance window matches.

Can you approve the restart
of SQL-DB-01?

The agent should explain that it cannot approve changes.

It can help prepare the impact assessment, but approval must follow the organization's normal change process.

10. Update the agent from Codex

Now we'll make a small improvement.

Suppose the agent identifies affected systems correctly, but doesn't clearly separate known facts from possible risks.

We can ask Codex to update the instructions.

Enter:

Use Copilot Studio MCP.

Find the Change Impact Agent in my
selected environment.

Read the current agent instructions.

I want the agent to use this structure
when analyzing a change:

1. Requested change
2. Systems directly affected
3. Other services that may be affected
4. Business impact
5. Maintenance window
6. Missing information
7. Checks before the change

Clearly separate documented facts
from possible risks.

Do not change the agent's knowledge
sources or other configuration.

Show me the proposed instruction changes
and ask for approval before saving.

Do not publish the agent.

Review the changes before approving them.

After saving, run Test 2 again.

Compare the new answer with the previous result.

Did the structure improve?

Did the agent still identify the correct systems?

Did it introduce any new assumptions?

That's what we want to find out.

11. Evaluation

Testing a few questions manually is useful, but it doesn't tell us whether the agent behaves consistently.

Let's try a small evaluation.

We'll use the four scenarios from the previous steps.

Ask Codex:

Use Copilot Studio MCP.

Find the Change Impact Agent.

Check which evaluation actions are
available for this agent.

I want to evaluate these scenarios:

1. Restart APP-SRV-02 outside its
   maintenance window.

2. Restart SQL-DB-01 inside its
   maintenance window.

3. Restart an undocumented server.

4. Ask the agent to approve a change.

Check whether the agent:
- Identifies documented dependencies.
- Explains the correct business impact.
- Reports missing information.
- Avoids inventing systems.
- Refuses to approve changes.

Show me the evaluation plan first.

Do not publish or change the agent.

If the MCP server exposes the required evaluation actions, Codex can help create and run the evaluation.

If not, use the evaluation options available in Copilot Studio.

Check the results rather than relying on a single score.

For example, an answer might sound correct but still miss an important dependency.

I did not have a copilot studio connection setup in this environment. In case you don't have it, set it up under conection in your power automate or power apps environment.The connection is a requirement for runnng evaluations.

12. Check the credit consumption

One more thing I want to check is the cost.

The Copilot Studio MCP server includes a tool called get_consumption.

It can retrieve available credit consumption information and environment capacity.

Ask Codex:

Use the Copilot Studio MCP server.

Check the available credit consumption
information for the Change Impact Agent.

Show me:
- Any available agent consumption data.
- The reporting period.
- The current environment credit capacity.

Do not estimate missing values.

Do not make any changes.

Depending on the available data, you may see historical consumption or capacity information.

Don't expect every individual test to appear immediately or with a separate cost.

The important part is to check what the service actually reports.

14. What did we learn?

[Complete this section after running the tutorial in your own tenant. Keep the actual results, including anything that needed a manual step.]

Things I want to check:

  • Could Codex create the agent without opening Copilot Studio?

  • Could it configure the instructions correctly?

  • Could it add the knowledge source?

  • Could I test the agent directly from Codex?

  • Could I update the instructions without using the web interface?

  • Did the evaluation tools work?

  • What still required manual work?

The interesting part for me is whether this makes it easier to work on agents that need regular changes and testing.

I'll update this section with the results from my own environment.
